newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine market mood not dented by general strike.
newsitem.headline: Argentine market mood not dented by general strike.

text.p: Argentine analysts said the general strike that plagued the country for a second day in a row Friday would not dent the firm underlying sentiment in financial markets.
"It hasn't and won't have any impact," said Peter Schubert, an analyst at Mexican brokerage Interacciones.
In fact on Thursday, when the 36-hour strike by trade unions protesting the government's economic policies kicked off at noon, bonds and stocks rose sharply.
Argentines will vote for 129 out of 257 representatives in the lower house of Congress in October next year.

But "the government is increasing pressures on Congress to pass important legislation quickly," said Roberto Costa Bourdieu, the senior fixed income analyst at Banco Ro de la Plata. "The government is firm in its conviction of its economic policies."

That means the government's planned labor reforms which are eyed eagerly by markets to lower governemnt expenditure and reduce costs for companies are likely to become law way before next year's elections.

The MerVal stock index of the 28 most-active stocks on Buenos Aires Stock Exchange rose 1.2 percent and Argentina's FRB advanced 1/8 Thursday. Markets slipped Friday but traders said that was due to a slowdown in the rally of U.S. Treasuries.
The biggest fear markets have had is that this second strike in two months could somehow slow the government's economic reforms.

But quite to the contrary the government announced yet another privatization on Thursday and late Wednesday Senate passed into law the long-awaited tax-hiking measures that are expected to generate some $1.6 billion in revenues to state coffers this year.

The Senate also authorized the government to sell another $4.0 billion of debt in 1996. The government quickly took advantage of that approval by announcing Friday it will issue a $750 million 10-year global bond.
"It is not an accident that (President Carlos) Menem is coming up with new things now," said Esteban Thomsen, Argentina economist at ING Barings.
Menem Friday dismissed the strike as a "complete failure."

The market's other big worry was that the strike could translate into defeat for the ruling Peronist Party at next year's mid-session congressional elections. That could make it much harder to get congressional support for unpopular laws.
Analysts are not sure this disatisfaction will move to the ballot box anyway. As Thomsen of ING Barings says: "This strike unifies a complaint, not a political opposition."
Apart from that, many of the sources of popular discontent such as the near-record unemployment rate of 17.1 percent that unions are protesting may ease as the buds of economic growth take root.
"Next year's election will depend a lot on economic growth which is picking up, so support could then return to the government," said Bourdieu.
"Growth will trickle down to confidence," said Thomsen.

What is more, argues Schubert of Interacciones, markets need not worry because the first strike in August, the blackout protest a couple of weeks ago and this strike, have not led to any concessions to the unions.
"It's going to be difficult to call a strike again, because of the lack of any real impact," he said.
--Buenos Aires Newsroom, 541 3180668
